Theodor Bibliander
tā'ō-dor bib-lē-an'der
n. (Theodor Bibliander, 1509–1564, Zwingli's successor in the Old Testament chair at Zurich, orientalist and editor of the first printed Qur'an)
Greek Theodoros, gift of God; Bibliander, a grecised form of his family name Buchmann, book-man.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Theodor Bibliander studied Hebrew under Pellikan and succeeded Zwingli in the Zurich chair of Old Testament in 1532, holding it for twenty-eight years. He was the first systematic comparative linguist of the age, publishing in 1548 a treatise comparing the grammar of the Semitic and other tongues; and in 1543 he brought out at Basel, after the city magistrates had imprisoned him for attempting it and Luther had written urging that it be allowed, the first printed edition of the Qur'an in Latin, with the argument that Christians cannot answer a religion they have not read. He was also one of the gentlest men of his century, and it cost him his chair. He resisted the hardening of the Zurich doctrine of predestination under Peter Martyr Vermigli's influence, holding to a more universal view of the offer of the gospel, and was pensioned off in 1560. The dictionary holds Zurich's doctrine and records Bibliander's principle on the Qur'an as sound. “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear” (1Pe 3:15).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an apology as a defence or vindication, and an orientalist as one versed in the eastern languages.

expand to see more

APOL'OGY, n. A defence or justification of what appears to others wrong; a vindication.

O'RIENTALIST, n. An inhabitant of the eastern parts of the world; one versed in eastern languages.

MEEK'NESS, n. Softness of temper; mildness; gentleness; forbearance under injuries.

COMPAR'ATIVE, a. Estimated by comparison; having the power of comparing.

Modern Corruption

The orientalist who printed the Qur'an so Christians could answer it.

expand to see more

Bibliander is now enlisted on both sides of a modern quarrel. He is cited as a pioneer of interfaith respect, as though his purpose in printing the Qur'an had been appreciation; and he is cited by others as proof that studying a false religion is the first step to excusing it. His own preface settles it: he printed the book so that its errors could be shown from its own pages, and he thought Christians disgraced themselves by refuting from rumour what they had never read.

The principle to recover is that an answer must be informed and civil without being soft: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear” (1Pe 3:15). Solomon states the rule Bibliander was applying to Islam and his opponents were breaking: “He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him” (Pro 18:13).

Usage

"“He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him” (Pro 18:13) — his argument to the magistrates."

"“speak forth the words of truth and soberness” (Act 26:25) — twenty-eight years in Zwingli's chair."
